1221.event_title: Hürrem Sultan's letters to Suleiman on campaign
1221.event: Hürrem, a captive Slavic woman who became the favourite and later the legal wife of the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, wrote him long letters whenever he was away on military campaigns. Historians describe these letters as filled with her love and longing for him, her distress at his absence and her prayers for his safety in battle.
1221.explanation: Her letters are one of the best-documented records from the early modern world of a wife's grief at a husband's long absence, written by the wife herself.
1221.tie_back: The kural calls the evening a killing time for wives whose husbands are away, and Hürrem's letters show exactly that kind of wife, consumed by grief while her husband was far off on campaign.
1221._accuracy_note: Strong match for a wife suffering her husband's absence, though the letters speak of grief day and night rather than of the evening hour in particular.

1222.event_title: Héloïse writes to Abelard of feeling neglected and forgotten
1222.event: After their love affair ended in separation, Héloïse entered the convent of Argenteuil and Peter Abelard became a monk; around 1126 Abelard handed over his foundation, the Paraclete, to Héloïse and her nuns. In the famous letters the two later exchanged, Héloïse called herself the most wretched and unhappy of women and told Abelard that she had been neglected and forgotten by him.
1222.explanation: The letters are among the most celebrated documents of medieval love, showing a woman who kept loving a partner she felt had grown distant.
1222.tie_back: The kural's wife asks whether the evening's partner is as hard-hearted as her own, and Héloïse likewise accused her beloved of neglecting her while she went on grieving for him.
1222._accuracy_note: The charge of a partner's hard-heartedness matches, but the kural's tender image of commiserating with the dim evening has no counterpart.

1223.event_title: Dante writes La Vita Nuova after the death of Beatrice
1223.event: As a boy of nine, Dante Alighieri glimpsed Beatrice Portinari and fell in love with her, and he remained in love with her until her death in 1290. Stricken with grief, he wrote La Vita Nuova (The New Life) around 1293, a book of sonnets and other poems linked by prose that traces his love from their first meeting through her death and his mourning.
1223.explanation: The book is a founding work of Italian literature and a lasting record of how grief for a lost beloved can grow and take over a life.
1223.tie_back: The kural describes sorrow budding and growing in the one left alone, and Dante's grief after Beatrice's death grew into a whole book of mourning.
1223._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shows grief for a lost beloved growing, but the loss is by death rather than a husband's absence and there is no evening imagery.

1224.event_title: The Blitz begins with an evening of bombing over London
1224.event: On Saturday 7 September 1940, starting around 4 pm, hundreds of German planes attacked the docks of east London, beginning the Blitz. London was then bombed for 57 nights in a row; blackout rules dimmed the city's lights, and within weeks about 120,000 people a night were sheltering in Underground stations.
1224.explanation: For Londoners in 1940 nightfall became the hour when the enemy arrived, so the coming of evening itself was something to dread.
1224.tie_back: The kural says that, without her beloved, evening approaches the wife like enemies advancing on a killing ground, and in the Blitz the coming of evening literally meant the coming of an enemy.
1224._accuracy_note: Next-best: it makes the image of evening arriving like an enemy literal, but it has nothing to do with love or separation.

1225.event_title: Michitsuna's Mother records lonely nights in the Kagerō Diary
1225.event: The Heian noblewoman known as Michitsuna's Mother recorded twenty years of her life, from 954 to 974, in the Kagerō Diary, centred on her marriage to the powerful courtier Fujiwara no Kaneie, which ended in divorce. One of her poems, later chosen as poem 53 of the anthology Hyakunin Isshu, describes lying alone through the hours of the night until daylight comes and asks whether anyone can understand how empty such a night is.
1225.explanation: The diary is one of the earliest autobiographies by a woman and gives a frank picture of a wife's long waits for a husband who seldom came.
1225.tie_back: The kural's wife finds the morning kind and the evening cruel, and this poet's most famous poem dwells on a night of lonely waiting that ends only when daylight comes.
1225._accuracy_note: Good match for a wife's dread of the lonely night and relief at daybreak, though the poem does not literally praise the morning.

1226.event_title: Maria Theresa goes into lifelong mourning for Francis Stephen
1226.event: In 1765 Emperor Francis Stephen died suddenly at Innsbruck, where the imperial family had gathered for the wedding of their son Leopold. His widow, Empress Maria Theresa, cut her hair short, wore widow's black for the rest of her life, largely withdrew from public life and gave up most of her jewellery. She lived about fifteen more years and was buried beside him in a double sarcophagus in the Capuchin crypt in Vienna.
1226.explanation: Her mourning is a well-documented example of a ruler whose life was visibly changed by the loss of her husband.
1226.tie_back: The kural's wife says she never knew such suffering while her husband was still at her side, and Maria Theresa's life after 1765 was marked by a grief she had not known while Francis Stephen lived.
1226._accuracy_note: The contrast between life with and without the husband fits, but the separation is death rather than absence and the evening theme is missing.

1227.event_title: Nizami completes the romance of Layla and Majnun
1227.event: The Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi completed his verse romance Layla and Majnun around 1188 as part of his Khamsa (Quintet), at the request of the Shirvanshah ruler. In the story Qays loves Layla so completely that he becomes known as Majnun, meaning madman; when her father refuses the match he flees into the desert, the thought of Layla keeps him awake at night, and after she dies of heartbreak he dies at her grave.
1227.explanation: The poem became the most influential love story of the Persian and wider Islamic world, the classic picture of love as a sickness that grows until it consumes the lover.
1227.tie_back: The kural shows love-sickness growing from bud to full flower as the day goes on, and Nizami's poem traces Majnun's love growing in the same way until it overwhelms him.
1227._accuracy_note: Next-best: the event is the writing of a poem about a legendary pair, and it shows love-sickness growing but not the kural's precise morning-to-evening cycle.

1228.event_title: Taps is first sounded at Harrison's Landing
1228.event: In July 1862, after the Seven Days battles, Union Brigadier General Daniel Butterfield had his brigade bugler Oliver W. Norton sound a new call in place of the usual Lights Out at the end of the day. The call, now known as Taps, spread through the Army of the Potomac and was soon being played at military funerals, and Army regulations made it mandatory at funerals in 1891. Some scholars think Butterfield revised an older call rather than composing it from scratch.
1228.explanation: A simple tune that marked the close of each day became, almost at once, the sound of mourning and loss.
1228.tie_back: The kural's herdsman's flute, which announces the evening, becomes a weapon that wounds the lonely wife, just as Taps, the bugle call of nightfall, became the call that announces grief.
1228._accuracy_note: A real piece of evening music that came to carry grief, a close parallel to the flute heralding painful dusk, though not tied to romantic separation.

1229.event_title: Nehru tells India the light has gone out after Gandhi's death
1229.event: At 5.17 pm on 30 January 1948, Mahatma Gandhi was shot and killed as he walked to his evening prayer meeting in the garden of Birla House, New Delhi. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, who had wept at the scene, spoke to the nation on All India Radio and told listeners that the light had gone out of their lives and there was darkness everywhere. The killing caused widespread shock and mourning across India and around the world.
1229.explanation: It is one of the clearest documented cases of a whole nation sharing one sudden grief as night fell.
1229.tie_back: The kural's wife feels that when evening spreads, the whole town is bewildered and grieving as she is, and on that evening in 1948 an entire country was plunged into shared grief and darkness.
1229._accuracy_note: Fits the picture of a whole town sharing grief at nightfall, but the grief is national mourning rather than a lover's longing.

1230.event_title: Gold Mountain wives wait in China for husbands working in America
1230.place: Southern China and the United States
1230.event: Many Chinese men went to work in the United States, which they called Gold Mountain, to earn money for their families, and laws such as the Page Law of 1875 and the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 kept most of them from bringing their wives. The wives who stayed behind, sometimes called grass widows or living widows, lived apart from their husbands for years or even decades, relying on letters and the money sent home.
1230.explanation: Their long separations show the human cost borne by families when husbands went abroad to earn a living.
1230.tie_back: The kural's wife pines at evening for a husband whose heart is set on earning wealth far away, which was the daily life of the Gold Mountain wives.
1230._accuracy_note: Very close fit: wives left alone for years while their husbands were away earning money, though individual evening laments are not recorded in the sources.
